II-H-01.note: B and C share an identical first clause, so the key cannot be picked on shape alone; C dies only on the absent chronology ('before the largest houses were built' is nowhere in the text). Best-built item in the main-idea block.

II-H-02.note: A inverts the text, B contradicts 'the grammatical spine is not [borrowed]', C invents a methodological complaint. D is the only scope-limited restatement and is selectable from the options alone.

II-H-03.note: C (mate attraction) and D (song learning) introduce topics no option-reader would expect a main-idea key to carry; A is the lone hedge.

II-H-04.note: C is the only option that limits itself to what each method can show; A, B, D each overreach in a way visible without the passage.

II-H-05.note: C is self-defeating (it asserts the daily rate fell, which no version of this passage would say alongside 'rising daily pay' in D). D recoverable from options alone.

II-H-06.note: B is the 'mostly explained away, small residue remains' hedge; A is a mechanism claim, C reverses the concrete/abstract finding, D is an unsupported scoring artifact.

II-H-07.note: D is genuinely defensible: 'the batons were made as working tools' is half the proposal, and polish from wood contact is direct evidence for it. A wins only because it also carries the 'saw use only rarely' half. A also sits slightly awry with the proposal's 'circulated mainly as marks of standing, seeing use only rarely' — under A the plainer batons show 'substantially heavier wear', i.e. not rare use. Deciding span: 'made as working tools but circulated mainly as marks of standing, seeing use only rarely.'

II-H-08.note: C is a clean exclusion experiment holding warmth constant; B actually favors the warming account, D is orthogonal to the north/south equality already stated.

II-H-09.note: B supplies physical traces of non-signatory readers, exactly what the register cannot record; A stays inside the register, C cuts against, D concerns duration not breadth.

II-H-10.note: B is defensible: an ant carried part of the way takes fewer steps and, on the step-counting account, should overshoot by less. It is weaker than D only because carriage does not hold gait, speed, or optic flow fixed. Deciding span: 'any of these could carry distance information just as well' — only D neutralizes one named alternative by design.

II-H-11.note: A is external documentary evidence and the only option that escapes the objector's circularity charge; B, C, D are all restatements of subject-matter or base-rate reasoning. Too transparent for the hard route.

II-H-12.note: C identifies the material as volcanic and matches a distant dated eruption, defeating the local-fire alternative; A and D both help the colleague, B is neutral.

II-H-13.note: A, B, C are each factually false against the four data points (transpiration falls monotonically; the 60% plot yielded 3.1 vs 4.1; the highest transpiration is the unshaded plot). No arithmetic required — pure fact-matching.

II-H-14.note: Requires computing 11.4x0.58=6.61 and 6.9x0.96=6.62. A and C are true statements that do not support equivalence; D is a near-miss (4.79 vs 6.9 is not 'about as much'). Strongest quantitative item in the set.

II-H-15.note: C is the only non-monotonic pair (38 burrows/9 cm vs 22/11). A is false at the third site; B is true but supports the opposite conclusion. The gravel-bar sentence is a live decoy that no option uses.

II-H-16.note: B is a good trap: a tenth of 9 is 0.9 and Program A's weakest gained 1, so it is false by 0.1. C is false (B's spread 9-10.4 is narrower) and D is false (A's 11 exceeds B's 10.4). A is the sample-size caution the analyst is making.

II-H-17.note: B captures the divergence (nitrogen 34-51-66-74 monotone; worms 62-78-71-39, ending below baseline). C is false, D's second clause is false (74 is not double 66), A is true but shows parallel movement, i.e. the opposite of the claim.

II-H-18.note: D pairs slowdown with recall gain per group, which is the stated conclusion. C is false (0.7 vs 0.1 is not 'about the same'), B is false (8 points vs 1), A is true but does not link slowing to retention.

II-H-19.note: The shared chromosomal region plus intact genes points to hitchhiking. B and D are absolutes and A asserts a chronology the text does not give; C is the only hedged option ('may be').

II-H-20.note: Textbook two-confounder setup with the 'cannot be separated on this evidence' option present. B, C, D each require a magnitude the text never supplies. Not a hard-route item.

II-H-21.note: C is the natural wrong answer and is killed by two spans working together: 'the tide there arrives progressively later as one moves south' (the offset is real, not error) and 'Nothing in either copy indicates that its scribe had seen the other's table.' Genuinely requires the passage.

II-H-22.note: A overreaches ('should vanish'), C invents an efficiency claim, D is a blanket refusal. B is the standard matched-comparison conclusion and is pickable from option shape.

II-H-23.note: The glue in the chalk ground absorbs UV, so survival is due to the substrate. B contradicts the open-southern-portico detail, C adds moisture from nowhere, D is garbled. A is the lone comparative hedge.

II-H-24.note: C is the scope-limiting restatement; A reverses the direction, B discards the wrong half, D is false since excluding trunks still leaves the sub-30cm reversal.
